title: Use after move
rustc:
error[E0382]: borrow of moved value: `note`
 --> example.rs:4:15
  |
2 |     let note = String::from("lunch");
  |         ---- move occurs because `note` has type `String`, which does not implement the `Copy` trait
3 |     let moved = note;
  |                 ---- value moved here
4 |     println!("{note} {moved}");
  |               ^^^^^^ value borrowed here after move
  |
help: consider cloning the value if the performance cost is acceptable
  |
3 |     let moved = note.clone();
  |                     ++++++++
explanation: A String owns its bytes. Assigning it to `moved` moves that ownership. `note` is empty afterward, so printing it is a use after move. `i32` would still work because it is `Copy` and the assignment copies the bits.

title: Two mutable borrows
explanation: `&mut` means exclusive access. Two mutable borrows at the same time could both change the vector, so the compiler stops you. Finish with the first borrow, then take the second.

title: Mutable borrow during a shared borrow
explanation: `view` is a shared borrow: it promises the vector will not change while it exists. `push` needs a mutable borrow. Using `view` afterward means the shared borrow is still alive, so the push is rejected. Read first, then mutate.

title: Mismatched types
rustc:
error[E0308]: mismatched types
 --> example.rs:2:23
  |
2 |     let amount: u64 = "12.50";
  |                 ---   ^^^^^^^ expected `u64`, found `&str`
  |                 |
  |                 expected due to this
explanation: "12.50" is text, a `&str`. A `u64` is an integer. Rust will not guess that you wanted cents. Parse the text, or store the minor units as a number from the start. This project parses the string into `Money` so the float never appears.

title: Trait not implemented
rustc:
error[E0277]: the trait bound `String: From<u64>` is not satisfied
 --> example.rs:3:33
  |
3 |     let display: String = cents.into();
  |                                 ^^^^ the trait `From<u64>` is not implemented for `String`, which is required by `u64: Into<_>`
  |
  = note: required for `u64` to implement `Into<String>`
explanation: `into()` only works when a `From` implementation exists for that pair of types. `String` implements `From<&str>`, not `From<u64>`. Numbers become text through `format!` or `Display`, which is what `Money` uses.

title: Method not found
rustc:
error[E0599]: no method named `as_dollars` found for struct `Money` in the current scope
 --> example.rs:5:26
  |
1 | struct Money(u64);
  | ------------ method `as_dollars` not found for this struct
...
5 |     println!("{}", money.as_dollars());
  |                          ^^^^^^^^^^ method not found in `Money`
explanation: Methods come from `impl` blocks. `Money` has no `as_dollars` method, so the call is a typo or a method you still need to write. The compiler lists the type so you can see where to add the `impl`.

title: Missing lifetime
rustc:
error[E0106]: missing lifetime specifier
 --> example.rs:2:11
  |
2 |     note: &str,
  |           ^ expected named lifetime parameter
  |
help: consider introducing a named lifetime parameter
  |
1 ~ struct Expense<'a> {
2 ~     note: &'a str,
  |
explanation: A reference inside a struct has to say how long it stays valid. Without a lifetime, the struct could outlive the text it points at. Naming the lifetime `'a` ties the struct to that borrow. Owned data (`String`) needs no lifetime, which is why the ledger stores notes as `Option<String>`.

title: Unused Result
rustc:
warning: unused `Result` that must be used
 --> example.rs:2:5
  |
2 |     std::fs::remove_file("this-file-is-not-created.txt");
  |     ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
  |
  = note: this `Result` may be an `Err` variant, which should be handled
  = note: `#[warn(unused_must_use)]` on by default
help: use `let _ = ...` to ignore the resulting value
  |
2 |     let _ = std::fs::remove_file("this-file-is-not-created.txt");
  |     +++++++
explanation: `remove_file` returns a `Result` because the file might not exist. Ignoring that value hides the failure. Handle it with `?` in a function that returns `Result`, or match on it. `let _ =` silences the warning only when you truly mean to ignore the error. The `spend` CLI prints `error: ...` instead of dropping the `Result`.
